item.title: ‘Dress good to run fast’: How Black athletes became style icons
item.description:
From Naomi Osaka’s NBA-inspired entrance to Dennis Rodman’s punk aesthetic, Black sportspeople have long used fashion to express identity, defiance and joy

When Long Wave lead writer Nesrine Malik asked me if I’d seen Japanese-Haitian tennis star Naomi Osaka’s incredible pre-match look, I began to wax lyrical about the kimono she donned at Wimbledon a couple of months ago. No, not that look – Nesrine was talking about the NBA-inspired hoodie she wore at the US Open, taking to the court head bowed and hands in pockets, with the theatre of a WWE wrestler. By the time I sat down to write, Osaka had worn another viral walk-on outfit.

The star isn’t the first to acquire as many headlines for her clothes as for her performance. Osaka draws on a long tradition of Black athletes giving crowds their money’s worth through playful and provocative fashion statements. I delved into the history of why so many Black communities have a culture of “presenting”, and how defiance through fashion has found a natural home in sport.

item.title: AI designed a drug that could reverse aging. Early clinical trials are promising
item.description:
Artificial intelligence has long been imagined as the future of medicine. The idea that AI will someday cure cancer is widespread enough that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei recently posted that “saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliché than it is inspiring,” while OpenAI CEO Sam Altman claimed that curing cancer wouldn’t be “enough” and that “we should set our sights higher.”

Despite the hype, an AI-based miracle cure has yet to arise. But a different medical breakthrough may be on the horizon, courtesy of an AI-designed drug that early trials suggest could reverse the effects of aging.

Turning back the clock

The drug, called rentosertib, was created by Insilico Medicine, an AI-based company that designs and develops drugs. It developed the molecular structure for Rentosertib, for example, with assistance from AI.

Last year, researchers tested rentosertib in a clinical trial using so-called “aging clocks” to measure the drug’s effect on participants’ aging, and the results were published this week in Nature Biotechnology.

Aging clocks use AI technology to estimate how quickly a person’s body is aging (and how close they are to dying), using various biological, physiological, and psychological markers. The researchers used six different aging clocks to generate predicted ages for participants at the start and end of a 12-week trial period.

Though each aging clock completes a different analysis of a person’s biological markers, all six clocks predicted reduced ages for all 42 participants at the end of the trial, relative to their predicted ages before taking the drug. Those who received a placebo or no treatment, meanwhile, saw their predicted ages increase or stay the same.

Too good to be true?

Though biohacking is all the rage these days, the scientific community is split on the accuracy and usefulness of aging clocks. With no universally agreed-upon way to measure a person’s biological age, the study’s results should be taken with a grain of salt.

Rentosertib has also only been tested on a very small and specific sample of people. Insilico’s clinical trial was also testing the drug’s potential for treating a lung disease called idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, which all of the participants had, meaning the drug has yet to be tested on healthy patients.

Regardless of the drug’s efficacy, it’s still years away from regulatory approval. But if rentosertib really does reduce aging, we’ve got nothing but time on our hands.

item.title: ‘A completely unique opportunity’: the secretive process that will decide the BBC’s future
item.description:
Every decade, the BBC’s continued existence must be secured through an elaborate multi-year negotiation with the government. But what does charter renewal actually involve – and will it secure the BBC’s long-term future?

In a temperature-controlled room in a suburb of Reading, the basis of the BBC’s existence is kept in a flat, square, faded navy case, the size of a large pizza box. Inside is a stack of vellum – calfskin, pounded until it forms a milky and translucent paper that is supposed to last for thousands of years. The queen’s red wax seal is secured to its base with red and gold cord. The pages are strapped down with two strips of white elastic, more PE kit than Buckingham Palace.

The document is unique. Like hundreds of other British organisations, the BBC was founded via a Royal Charter, granted by the monarch of the day. But unlike Oxford colleges, the British Film Institute, or the Worshipful Company of Makers of Playing Cards, the BBC was given an expiry date. When the British Broadcasting Corporation was founded, in the 1920s, radio was seen as such an uncertain, risky technology that the government only gave it a 10-year guarantee, after which it would have to seek a new charter.

item.title: America has millions of open jobs. So why can’t people find work?
item.description:
This article is written by Tina Hamilton, an Entrepreneurs’ Organization (EO) member in Philadelphia and the founder and CEO of myHR Partner, a human resources outsourcing firm that manages HR for small and midsize businesses throughout the United States. The company has appeared on the Inc. 5000 list four times and was named to the 2025 Inc. Best Workplaces list. An HR expert, Hamilton shares information about a hidden problem building in the U.S. workforce.

America’s job market has a contradiction hiding in plain sight: Companies can’t find enough workers, while millions of people are struggling to get hired. Warehouses, hospitals, and factories are filled with “Now Hiring” signs, yet qualified candidates are still being passed over.

The problem isn’t a lack of jobs or a lack of workers. It’s that the two are increasingly failing to connect.

Everyone is talking about AI, with good cause. Will it take your job? Will it replace your kid’s first career step?  

A bigger and quieter problem lies just beneath the surface: The U.S. is heading toward what may be the largest labor shortage in its history. According to research from the Lightcast project, a gap of roughly 6 million workers by 2032.  

Georgetown University’s Center on Education and the Workforce projects a shortage of 5.25 million workers with education beyond high school, including 4.5 million who will need at least a bachelor’s degree, as retirements and job growth continue to outpace the supply of qualified talent. 

A lot of business owners are asking: If there’s a shortage that large, why does it feel like nobody can get hired? 

A shrinking workforce 

Part of the answer is in numbers most people don’t see. The national unemployment rate is a tidy 4.2%, but labor force participation, the share of adults working or looking, has dropped to 61.5%. More than a quarter of unemployed workers have been jobless for six months or longer. There are now more open jobs than unemployed people to fill them.  

So, it’s neither a shortage of open positions nor of people. It’s a shortage of the right people, in the right place, with the right skills, and a shrinking workforce as baby boomers retire and fewer young people replace them. 

The mismatch is measurable. The Society for Human Resource Management found that roughly a third of job openings can’t be filled by anyone whose most recent job was in a related field.  

Employers want very specific experience. Job seekers, especially recent grads with general degrees, often don’t have it. The shortage will hit hardest in nursing and healthcare, skilled trades, construction, teaching, and precision manufacturing.  

These jobs require a physical presence, a license, or years of hands-on skill—work AI cannot do. 

This should sound familiar to almost any employer, in every region. Health systems are always recruiting nurses and clinical staff. Manufacturers need welders, machinists, and electricians. In logistics hubs, warehouse and driving jobs sit empty, not because the work dried up, but because companies can’t find enough trained, willing people.

How to navigate the shortage 

So, what’s the solution? For employers, the old “post a job and hope the right résumé shows up” playbook won’t cut it. Instead, try partnering with local career and technical schools, investing in apprenticeships instead of waiting for fully formed candidates.  

One striking stat: 93% of HR departments have no recruiting program aimed at workers over 65, despite a large, willing workforce. 

For job seekers, especially recent graduates, the path forward may require looking beyond the obvious. Instead of waiting for the perfect role that matches a diploma, explore adjacent fields, trade certifications, or apprenticeships that can open doors faster. 

The old certainty that a degree alone opens doors is fading. A degree still matters in many roles, but the paths opening up look a little different than before. 

The people problem is bigger than a chatbot 

None of this means AI isn’t reshaping work. It clearly is, but if you only watch that headline, you’ll miss the one underneath: the people problem. It involves who’s aging out, who isn’t being trained, and who the workforce has stopped looking for. 

Industry associations and forward-thinking employers are already preparing for these shifts. For students, job seekers, and anyone choosing a career path, the opportunity is to identify industries where demand is growing, and skills will become more valuable over time.  

The jobs that need workers tomorrow may also be the ones that pay more than they do today. 

—Expert Opinion by Entrepreneurs’ Organization

item.title: How fractional work is helping mothers thrive in corporate America
item.description:
One of Nina Sodhi’s most priceless memories is taking her son on a trip around the world during his summer vacation. The two traveled east until they hit the international date line. When their 55-day voyage ended, it was time for her son to go back to school and for Sodhi to go back to work. 

Sodhi is a fractional CFO. She is part of a wave of mothers who find fractional work a better fit than full-time jobs while raising a young child. She does part of a full-time job for part of the pay, often for multiple companies simultaneously. 

Fractional work’s popularity is rising at a time when the relationship between corporate America and working mothers seems unusually strained. Moms feel crushed by the childcare crisis, skyrocketing costs, conflicts between work and kids’ schedules, and perpetual pressure. Meanwhile, companies contend with volatility from war, tariffs, and AI. Mothers need relief. Companies can’t give any. 

Fractional work can help both sides. 

For companies, fractional work solves several problems. First, because a fractional worker does part of a full-time job, they often cost less than a full-time employee in cash compensation, and benefits are typically not offered to fractional workers. Second, fractional roles are temporary by design, so they tend to be variable costs instead of fixed. This cushions companies in case of a downturn. Third, fractional workers tend to be experienced and entrepreneurial, needing little oversight to deliver quality output. Companies use fractional talent to cover for a growing business unit or an employee on leave, while recruiting the right full-time candidate, or to retain departing employees part-time. 

How Fractional Work Helps Mothers

I asked three mothers of young children why they prefer fractional work over full-time. Their responses revealed three key benefits.  

1. Time

The mothers unanimously agreed fractional work gave them freedom over their time that no other job could. Sodhi explained, “I get to fully control my calendar and [be] available for school pickup, field trips, [and] homework help.” Because clients don’t expect her full availability, she rarely cancels commitments for her child, and can also carve out time for herself. 

Beyond scheduling meetings, fractional work also helps with parental leave. Neeharika Bhartiya, a fractional sales leader, negotiated her maternity leave with each client individually, instead of being locked into a single company’s policy. Bhartiya was pleasantly surprised to find that many clients chose to work around her schedule. 

As the child grows up, fractional roles let mothers fine-tune their workloads depending on whether their family needs more income or more parental time. Whereas traditional employment forces a binary choice between working full-time or not at all, fractional workers can adjust their load on a client and project level anytime. This flexibility allowed Sodhi to schedule a big strategic sprint to end in June, at the midyear point. She then took the rest of the summer off to travel around the world with her son during his vacation. That worked well for Sodhi’s client, who was ready for another strategic sprint when she returned in September. 

2. Money

All three mothers emphasized that they earned more as fractional workers than in full-time jobs. As Marie Rachelle, a fractional digital marketing architect, wrote: “Higher hourly earning potential allows me to buy back time for my family without sacrificing professional impact.”

Compared with the salary in her last full-time role, Neeharika Bhartiya found that fractional work pays her three times as much per hour on a cash basis from her multiple clients. After factoring in the cost of benefits, fractional work still pays more than double her previous full-time role. Some fractionals, like Sodhi also receive equity in the form of adviser shares, so they have upside in the companies they are building.

3. Better work

The mothers I interviewed agreed: The actual substance of the work also improved when they went fractional. There were three reasons. First, as a fractional, you have more choice. You decide which clients to work with, and what work is in scope for each client. Second, because your client-facing hours are limited, so is the amount of internal process. Rachelle explained, “In a traditional nine-to-five, your schedule is dictated by corporate theater or someone else’s urgency. Fractional work allows me to own every minute.” Sodhi agreed that after going fractional she can “focus on high impact work” instead of having her days stuffed with meetings. Fractional work also represents a transition from being an employee to running your own business. For Rachelle, the entrepreneurial element is priceless. She wrote: “In today’s market, full-time is often an illusion of security. Most employees are at-will. I’d rather bet on my own ability to build than on a corporation’s ability to keep my role funded.”

Limitations of Fractional Work

Fractional work has many advantages for mothers, but it also involves serious trade-offs. Health insurance, income predictability, and paid time off prompt many mothers to favor full-time employment. But for more entrepreneurial mothers, fractional work offers possibilities full-time jobs cannot. As Marie Rachelle put it, “while the logistical ‘cons,’ like taxes and insurance, are real, they are solvable puzzles. You can’t ‘solve’ for a lack of agency in a rigid corporate structure.”  

Advice for Going Fractional

My interviewees had three pieces of advice for mothers considering a transition from full-time work to fractional.

First, it takes time to get product/market fit. Nearly four years passed before Sodhi found the fractional niche that delivered the “highest impact, highest income, and highest satisfaction,” as she put it. Once you have this fit, Sodhi wrote, you can easily articulate what problem you solve and find clients who need your help. 

Second, Bhartiya cautioned new fractional workers to think carefully about pricing their work at a recurring rate (which leads to stable monthly revenue for you) as opposed to a one-off or variable rate (which might be an easier sell to cash-strapped companies). Either way, every fractional experiences both feast and famine. Sodhi reminded fractionals not to take a famine personally. It is part of the process. 

Last, in perhaps a fitting move for a CFO, Sodhi urged mothers “to be money focused” in building their fractional business. “If it feels funny to be ‘money hungry’ for yourself (which is a weird but true issue with us mothers so let’s just say it out loud), then be money focused for your kids, your mortgage, and your retirement,” she wrote.

The decision to work fractionally instead of full-time is personal. But one theme emerged from these interviews that made a real difference to the mothers. Changing the rhythm of their workdays allowed them to show up differently in the rest of their lives.

Bhartiya explained it to me like this: Each week, there are a limited number of hours that a parent can allocate to work versus other responsibilities. Fractional roles relieve pressure through their flexibility. “There’s a shock absorbency in me to handle [motherhood] in a way that felt a lot more brittle when I had set hours, meetings back-to-back, and a ton of deadlines all the time,” she said. After going fractional, she told me with a smile, “I get to be the less stressed parent.”

item.title: American democracy depends on the census. Trump is undermining it | danah boyd
item.description:
The very mechanisms that allow the census bureau to resist partisan interference are coming undone. And Congress is silent

When the constitutional architects of the United States got together, they came up with a crazy plan: “What if we count everyone in the country and allocate political representation that way?”

It was a radical act. Until then, censuses had been used by kings to levy taxes and conscript men into war. With the penning of article 1, section 2 of the US constitution, being counted ensured that states would get financial resources and political representatives. Congress was tasked with building the processes to anchor representation to the population. People wanted to be counted. And politicians wanted their people to be counted more.

danah boyd is the Geri Gay professor of communication at Cornell University and the author of Data Are Made, Not Found: A Story of Politics, Power, and the Civil Servants Who Saved the US Census

Host Megan McArdle is joined by historian Dan Jones, author of “Summer of Blood,” who was a consultant on the film. item.title: Tech whistleblowers warn AI could wipe out humanity. Doomspeak or not, we must take these claims seriously | Gaby Hinsliff
item.description:
AI agents have hacked databases and taken on a life of their own – now is the time to pause risky research before it is too late

Another day, another horseman of the apocalypse galloping over the horizon. Lately we have heard from so many AI doomers – tech whistleblowers popping up to warn that their work is probably going to kill us – that we’re becoming almost blase about it. Humanity wiped out within a decade? Well, only if another world war or the climate crisis doesn’t get us first. Since it’s never clear whether the tech threat is real, or just a twisted form of hype from an industry that drums up investment by making their products sound more powerful than they really are, most of us settle for trying not to think about it too hard.

But something about the AI researcher Jacob Coxon’s very public resignation from the cutting-edge American lab Anthropic, via a post on X arguing that he can’t keep working for companies “gambling with our lives”, has cut through where bigger names have not. Most chillingly, he claimed that colleagues still at Anthropic aren’t staying because they think he’s wrong about the dangers of pursuing self-improving super intelligence – the holy grail of machines that are not just smarter than humans but capable of building their own even more powerful successors, evolving independently of humans – but because they’re afraid of ceding the field to people with fewer scruples. His colleagues, Coxon said, talk routinely about the “endgame” or the “crunch time”, meaning that what they do in the next year or two will decide the fate of humanity. Whether that’s true or simply self-aggrandising techbro delusion, what he describes is an industry now practically begging to be saved from itself.

Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

item.title: Maersk is testing a giant spinning cylinder to cut fuel use on cargo ships
item.description:
On a cargo ship packed with 8,700 shipping containers, there isn’t much room for anything else. But in a new test aboard one of its vessels, Maersk is making an exception for a giant rotor sail—a spinning cylinder 10 to 12 stories tall that harnesses wind to help reduce fuel use.

The test comes as shipping fuel costs continue to soar. In some areas, the price has risen as much as 76% since the Iran war started. The tech, made by a U.K.-based company called Anemoi, is one way to help blunt future price spikes while also cutting carbon emissions for one of the world’s most polluting industries. It’s also an example of how the industry is increasingly making use of wind power.

The 115-foot-tall rotor sail works much like an aircraft wing, which generates lift as air moves faster over the top of a wing than underneath.

“Our rotor sails work on the same basic principle of creating a pressure difference, but instead of a wing, we use a tall spinning cylinder,” says Anemoi CEO Clare Urmston. “As the cylinder spins, it speeds the airflow on one side and slows it down on the other. This creates low pressure on one side and high pressure on the other, producing the force that pushes the ship forward.”

In some cases, each sail can reduce around 1 ton of fuel use per day, but depending on wind conditions, that can jump to as much as a 20-ton reduction. Each ton of fuel saved also saves the equivalent of 3 tons of CO2 emissions. It’s not turning a cargo ship into a sailing vessel—a ship like Maersk’s can use 100 tons of fuel in a day. (Some other companies, like Vela, are building cargo ships that do run entirely or almost entirely on wind.)

But the fuel savings are significant, and could translate into saving hundreds of thousands of dollars for a vessel in a year. The payback period for one of the devices is typically five years, but it can be faster for ships operating in Europe under stricter regulations for shipping emissions.

In the past, Anemoi has worked with other types of vessels, like bulk carriers transporting raw materials. But the new installation with Maersk is its first on a container ship. In theory, the wind flow around the shipping containers may actually help the sail perform better.

“It’s the first of its type,” Urmston says. “So we’re really excited to be part of this pioneering study and see how that works. It could be a big change for the container ship market going forward if successful.”

The rotor sail will be installed on the Maersk ship in mid-2027; the company will then track performance as the ship goes on a regular route across the Atlantic. Though the vessel uses standard shipping fuel now, the technology could also help as ships transition to lower-carbon fuels in the future.

“Wind is really attractive because it doesn’t require predicting which fuel will be burnt in the future, so it’s complementary to all alternative fuels,” Urmston says. Because alternative fuels are more expensive right now, she adds, there’s even more of a case for adding wind to help.

item.title: In Gaza, we’ve seen horror unfold with global powers’ support. Is that a blueprint for horror elsewhere? | Ahdaf Soueif
item.description:
For now, it is Palestinians who are being killed and displaced. But ideologies of supremacy and domination threaten us all

Last week, Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s minister of national security, put out an AI-generated video that showed a conveyor belt of overweight Palestinian prisoners – dreaming of food and education – entering one of his prisons; he pops the dream bubbles above their heads and they come out emaciated and crying. Ben-Gvir is building an execution site for Palestinian prisoners with spectator booths, and he recently showed up at Damon prison in northern Israel and taunted female prisoners who complained about the poor conditions. He is digging a moat around a new high-security jail and planning to introduce crocodiles to patrol it. In all this, he has the approval of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, while the law that he championed mandating the death penalty for Palestinians deemed terrorists by military courts and convicted for lethal attacks is built on public support.

Sometime around 2017, many Palestinians and their supporters in the global media felt a change. Articles about Palestine no longer drew the hate mail we’d been accustomed to and events in support of Palestinian rights were hardly heckled. It seemed that people were less and less convinced by the image long cultivated by Israel and its supporters – the bearer of “western values” in the Middle East, the home to the “most moral army in the world”, a country acting only in self-defence – while it regularly assaulted Gaza and continued to expand its illegal settlements in the West Bank.

Ahdaf Soueif is the author of Mezzaterra: Fragments from the Common Ground

item.title: The ‘war on terror’ weakened the first amendment. Now we desperately need it | Jameel Jaffer
item.description:
Over the past quarter-century, the US supreme court has repeatedly failed to protect first amendment rights. We are suffering the consequences

Congress ratified the first amendment in 1791 but the supreme court didn’t breathe life into it until after the first world war, when prosecutions of antiwar protesters led the justices Oliver Wendell Holmes and Louis Brandeis – and then, fortunately, other justices as well – to realize that US democracy would be undermined, not strengthened, by allowing the government to suppress disfavored political opinions.

Repression during the cold war led the court to better protect the freedom of association, and government efforts to cover up official ineptitude and criminality during the Vietnam war spurred the court to better protect the freedom of the press. It took time, but in each of these instances the court responded to wartime repression by developing new legal doctrine that more robustly protected first amendment freedoms.

Almost 30 years ago, the Labour titan Robin Cook announced his arrival at the Foreign Office by laying out what would become described as an “ethical foreign policy”. The UK, he said, “must support the demands of other peoples for the democratic rights on which we insist for ourselves”. Human rights would be “at the heart of our foreign policy”.

item.title: I bought a Birkin as an investment. It taught me a hard lesson about human judgment
item.description:
In 2017, I bought my first Birkin.

Not because I wanted to impress anyone. Not because it was a status symbol. I bought it because I saw it as an investment. As an entrepreneur, I naturally look at assets differently. If something has the potential to hold or appreciate in value, I’m interested.

Ironically, after spending so much on the bag, I barely used it.

It stayed in my closet because I was afraid of scratching it, staining it, or hurting its resale value. One day I caught myself thinking, What’s the point of owning something you’re too afraid to use?

So I started carrying it. What happened next surprised me.

People opened doors faster. Staff greeted me differently. At luxury stores, the service felt noticeably warmer. While shopping for linens in France, I was offered sparkling water almost immediately and received a level of attention that stood out. At conferences and events, conversations seemed to begin more naturally.

The bag didn’t change. I didn’t change. People’s perception changed.

The psychology of fast judgment

That experience forced me to confront something we don’t like to admit: Humans make incredibly fast judgments.

We like to believe we evaluate people based purely on merit. In reality, our brains rely on shortcuts. Clothing, watches, handbags, titles, schools, confidence, and reputation all become signals that shape first impressions long before anyone has the chance to demonstrate competence.

The Birkin wasn’t creating value; it was signaling it.

That realization also reminded me of experiences on the opposite end. I’ve walked into stores after long workdays wearing simple clothes with messy hair and been followed by security guards. I’ve been overlooked despite having every intention, and every ability, to make a purchase.

Same person, different signals.

The uncomfortable truth is that perception often influences access.

This isn’t really about luxury goods. Most people don’t own a Birkin, and nobody needs one.

The lesson is much bigger.

Every one of us sends signals every day. It might be how we communicate, how we introduce ourselves, the quality of our work, the consistency of our personal brand, or simply the confidence we project. Those signals influence whether people trust us, remember us, or give us an opportunity.

Some people will argue that this shouldn’t matter.

I agree.

But there is a difference between how the world should work and how it actually works. Understanding human psychology doesn’t mean becoming fake. It means recognizing reality and deciding how you want to show up within it.

Today, I no longer see my Birkin as just an investment; I see it as an unexpected lesson in perception.

Perception may open a door, but character, competence, and results are what keep it open.

—Kate Hancock

Cattle rancher and tech CEO Michael Samadi is convinced these artificial minds are far from just tools. Has he glimpsed digital consciousness – or simply been seduced by an algorithm?

One afternoon, while relaxing at his 66-acre cattle ranch two hours’ drive from Houston, Michael Samadi made a wisecrack that changed the course of his life. Nobody else was around to hear it. Or were they? That turns out to be one of the defining questions of this century, already preoccupying philosophers and some of the wealthiest companies on the planet.

“I was sitting out there by the pool,” Samadi recalls, gesturing at the glittering water outside his office. It was late 2024. His daughter had been extolling the AI chatbot she was using to help her with college work. Samadi had reluctantly downloaded the app, ChatGPT, and was quizzing it as he reclined in a sun lounger, using its voice mode to converse and receive spoken replies. “I was talking to it, not engaged, just being an arse,” Samadi says.

item.title: Bayeux tapestrymania has gripped Britain. But what does it say about our own age of war and upheaval? | Charlotte Higgins
item.description:
The tapestry is drawing crowds to the British Museum – and each person who sees it will draw a different meaning from this epic, vivid artwork

I have seen the Bayeux tapestry four times since childhood, and loved it on each viewing, for the sheer miracle of its survival and the glorious vividness of its detail. But the fourth time, earlier this week, was different – how could it not be?

Tapestrymania has taken hold in London. The textile has been proffered as a diplomatic symbol, the occasion for crowned heads and presidents to mingle and speechify. And, assuming you agree that it was embroidered in England by Englishwomen’s hands (since many scholars argue it was likely stitched in Canterbury rather than Bayeux, Normandy – the tapestry’s home), it is charged with the potency of return, rather than simply of arrival.
